lines.text: Wartime wedding rings carried a Utility stamp.
In 1942, a British order limited how wedding rings were made.
lines.say: In nineteen forty two, a British order limited how wedding rings were made.

lines.text: They could only be 9 carat gold, not the usual 22 carat.
lines.say: They could only be nine carat gold, not the usual twenty two carat.

lines.text: A ring could weigh no more than two pennyweights.
Every legally made ring was stamped with a Utility mark.
Couples married in such numbers that rings ran short.
People waited, or bought second hand rings.
The London Assay Office kept hallmarking all through the war.
Its Utility punch was kept, though punches are normally destroyed.
A copy of it is still held at Goldsmiths' Hall in London.

post.caption: Wartime wedding rings carried a Utility stamp. In 1942, a British order limited how wedding rings were made. They could only be 9 carat gold, not the usual 22 carat. A ring could weigh no more than two pennyweights. Every legally made ring was stamped with a Utility mark. Couples married in such numbers that rings ran short. People waited, or bought second hand rings. The London Assay Office kept hallmarking all through the war. Its Utility punch was kept, though punches are normally destroyed. A copy of it is still held at Goldsmiths' Hall in London.
